steps.explanationAfterStep: No carbocation forms, so nothing rearranges. Boron at the less substituted carbon is preferred both for sterics and for the small positive charge building up on the middle carbon.

title: Hydroboration of propene
subtitle: B–H adds in one four-centre step
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 19

product.caption: propylborane (it goes on to react with two more propenes)

reactants.caption: propene + borane
hintTiers: Boron has only six electrons and an empty orbital. What will it accept?
The π bond gives its electrons to boron at the CH₂ end, while a B–H bond delivers its H to the middle carbon. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: from the C=C π bond to boron, forming a bond from the CH₂ carbon to B. Arrow 2: from a B–H bond to the middle carbon, forming a C–H bond.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Borane adds across the C=C bond. Draw the single concerted step.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Boron goes to the less hindered CH₂ end. In the transition state the partial positive charge is then on the middle carbon, which stabilises it better.
The H goes to the middle carbon. Boron, the bulkier end of B–H, bonds to the less hindered CH₂ carbon.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right start. Without a second arrow you would make a carbocation; instead, in the same step, a B–H bond delivers its H to the middle carbon.

mechanismSummary: Boron's empty p orbital accepts the π electrons while a hydrogen moves from boron to the other carbon, all in one step. Boron goes to the less hindered CH₂ end and H to the middle carbon: the opposite orientation to HBr. B and H add to the same face (syn). Each B–H bond reacts in turn, so BH₃ ends up as tripropylborane.
